We also began to see how it responds to a question that the historian studying from the outside cannot help asking. It is a question that has given rise to several schools within Shiism: among the immense and not always clearly bounded corpus of hadîth and akhbâr, which traditions should be judged “sound” (sahîh) and which “weak” (za'îf)? Which should be accepted, treated with reserve, or set aside? The position of Shaykhism is remarkably firm.

More precisely, it insists on separating that question from another, more essential one: the meaning and content (ma'nâ) of a hadîth or khabar itself. To see exactly what is at issue, we need only recall that the Shaykhis have often been accused of accepting “weak” traditions as valid.

Sarkâr Âghâ replies (pp. 237 ff.) by asking: what exactly are these supposedly weak traditions? The technical terminology used to classify traditions and grade their reliability is no more than about six centuries old. Before it was devised, what standard did people use to accept or reject the traditions? They must have had one; it is inconceivable that the prophetic religion was ever without such a standard.

By what right, then, and in the name of what authority, should we abandon that earlier measure, whose origins go back to the Prophet and the Imams, in favor of a later critical terminology and the criteria it imposes? If a tradition agrees with the Book and with the Sonnât jâmi'a—the “complete Tradition,” meaning, in Shiite usage, the whole body of traditions tracing back to the Prophet and the Imams—what principle requires us to reject it, even when the newer terminology pronounces its historical chain of transmission “weak”? That weakness is more than compensated for by the agreement itself. One may certainly acknowledge that some narrators and transmitters (rowât, rijâl) are more trustworthy than others.

But these men were not prophets, whereas the Prophet and the Imams knew the invisible, suprasensory world. On the question of who may be trusted, specialists in the historical study of transmitters (rijâl) have filled books with conflicting judgments. Surely the assent of faith, the believer’s confidence in the Imams’ words, cannot depend on whether these critics approve or reject them.

Do these experts not place excessive confidence in their own discipline and its subject matter? Once we admit that someone might have been bold enough to fabricate a hadîth, why stop there? Why not admit that he might equally have fabricated an impeccable chain of authorities, all apparently beyond reproach, and so disarmed historical criticism in advance? (p. 240).

Here the same argument reappears that we encountered in the discussion of taqlîd. To accept the judgments of specialists in the study of transmitters would simply mean resting one’s faith on the human authority of the “transmitters,” rather than on the spiritual authority inherent in what the text teaches.

But the authority to which one turns and entrusts oneself is not that of a Mojtahed or a transmitter (râwî). It is the authority of the Imams—or, more precisely, of the “Imam who is invisible to the senses but present in the hearts of those who follow him.” From this point of view, there is no difference between the past and the present. The question of recognizing the Imam’s words and teaching remains the same then as now; time changes nothing.

The Imam’s presence is unchanged, and assent (tasdîq) depends ultimately not on any external human authority but on the testimony the Imam bears to himself in the heart of the believer. This is precisely what Shaykh Ahmad meant when he said he could “recognize an Imam’s hadîth by its fragrance.” There are no rational proofs to support such assent, but neither are there any that can disprove it. Negative philosophical criticism has no purchase here.

By contrast, philosophy’s task is without limit when it devotes itself to interpreting symbols. Sarkâr Âghâ expressly emphasizes that his purpose is not that of a historian: he does not claim to be practicing historical criticism. The point is precisely that assent to the beliefs of faith ('aqâ'id) can depend neither in principle nor in lived experience on criticism of that kind, for this would ultimately make it subordinate to some human authority (pp. 241–243). This shows how grave is the problem that Shaykhism has knowingly taken upon itself, fully aware of difficulties long familiar to Western theology and philosophy.

A revealing illustration is furnished by an anecdote, whether true or invented, about a certain Shaykh Mohammad Hasan at Najaf. A specialist solely in jurisprudence, but a formidable debater, he is said to have decided to test Shaykh Ahmad’s “sense of smell” (shamm), his capacity to recognize a tradition.

Tonkâbûnî recounts the episode; but, as we know, his sources are highly questionable. It also seems altogether improbable that the shaykh of Najaf would have allowed himself to behave in such a way. Whatever the truth, the story must be reported with scrupulous accuracy, not in an approximate version that tries to make it “more amusing” and, one fears, betrays an intention to ridicule Shaykh Ahmad. For here the inaccuracy leads to an utter confusion of two quite different questions.

Shaykh Mohammad Hasan supposedly “fabricated” a hadîth in elaborate Arabic, but supplied no isnâd, or chain of transmission. He then showed the paper to Shaykh Ahmad and said, “I have discovered a hadîth. Can you tell whether it really is a hadîth and understand its meaning (ma'nâ)?” It was the meaning and content that Shaykh Ahmad affirmed. His response is readily understood, since he had not been asked whether the chain of transmission was “sound” or “weak.”

To make a judgment using those labels, in the only sense to which they properly apply, no “divining faculty” is required: one simply has to identify the actual transmitters (rowât and rijâl). There are, in fact, two questions of entirely different kinds. One is a matter of historical criticism and belongs to the study of transmitters; the other concerns essence and spiritual meaning.

Or are we to assume that when a modern historian declares a hadîth “weak,” he does so because he finds its content unacceptable—for instance, a tradition concerning the ma'âd, the return in resurrection, or the “resurrection body”? If that is what he is doing, he should at least have the courage to say openly what standard he is using (pp. 251–252). Sarkâr Âghâ therefore sums up the problem in terms of decisive importance for every aspect of Shiite theology.

There are two paths, pursued by different people. 1) One may investigate the circumstances of the transmitters (rowât), as the Osûlîs do, and judge the “strength” or “weakness” of a “chain of transmission” according to the trustworthiness of those involved. This inquiry rests in turn on opinions expressed in historical works dealing with transmitters (rijâl) and traditionists (mohaddîthîn). It is the outward path, the external or exoteric method (râh-e zâhirî). It offers useful assistance, an auxiliary discipline, and enables one to form an opinion.

But it cannot lead to certainty about a truth of essence. 2) The second path aims precisely at that essential truth (râh-e haqîqî): the inward truth, the meaning and spiritual reality of what is said and signified. It asks whether what a hadîth or khabar says agrees with the explicit or implicit meaning of the Book and of the complete Tradition (sonnât) of the Prophet and the Imams.

Thus the shaykh consciously and unmistakably draws a distinction. On one side stands the knowledge produced by historical criticism, which remains external and is appropriate to a fides historica, a faith founded on historical evidence, but is insufficient in itself either to ground or to overturn the assent of lived spiritual faith.

On the other stands what we might call an intuition of essence—a phenomenological insight—which seeks to bring meaning and content to light and to perceive whether they harmonize with, or contradict, the whole symphony. Such perception admittedly presupposes a prior intuition of the meaning of that whole, and may be qualitative rather than quantitative. For this reason, it is explicitly said to be beyond the reach of just any learned person. It belongs only to those who possess spiritual capacity (qowwat-e qodsîya) and know the Imams’ way of speaking.

Indeed, a saying of the Sixth Imam states: “We do not recognize any one of you as learned until he has become able to recognize any of our hadîth that is presented to him” (p. 253). It is by this second path that meaning and content—significance and essence—are recognized, even where the Imam spoke in circumstances beyond the reach of external historical criticism. That, and nothing else, is what Shaykh Ahmad’s intuition could “recognize by its fragrance,” and what it did recognize.

This means that, even if the words had been invented by the person questioning him, they could still have agreed with the tradition; and in this case their meaning and content did in fact agree with the complete Tradition (sonnât jâmi'a). That said, it remains improbable that one of the religious scholars ('olamâ') would have indulged in such a game.

The fact that Shaykh Ahmad recognized the meaning is therefore all the less surprising, since it is even less conceivable that a scholar would have dared to fabricate a “false” saying that contradicted the Book and the sonnât jâmi'a (ibid.). The question put to Shaykh Ahmad thus amounted to something very simple. In any case, to recount the anecdote as though he had been asked to judge the validity or weakness of the historical chain of transmission, rather than the meaning and content, is—deliberately or not—to distort radically what happened.

We need not pursue the matter further. The saying of the Sixth Imam quoted a few lines above defines the position of Shaykhism and shows where it stands. That position requires, and gives a precise meaning to, a personal relationship of faith—and therefore a spiritual relationship—with the Imam as present now.

The certainty this relationship confers is of an entirely different order from anything that external historical research into the transmitters (rijâl) can provide. It gives that certainty a character independent of every external and temporal authority. The Imam, as the spiritual pole (qotb), gives the believer a “polar dimension.”

The frequent discussions of this question in Iran often leave one with the impression that the assumptions on either side have not been made sufficiently clear. Here, terminology developed in the West out of a comparable situation may help bring some clarity.

At the beginning of his own commentary on his book of Teachings (Fawâ'id), Shaykh Ahmad makes this declaration: “Whatever certainty I possess in my knowledge I owe to the Imams who guide us (A'immat al-hodâ). If my writings are free from error, it is because everything I affirm in my books comes from their teaching, and because they themselves are protected (ma'sûm) from error, omission, and missteps. Whoever allows himself to be taught by them can be sure of not going astray, so long as he follows them. This is the spiritual meaning of the Qur'anic verse (34:17): ‘Travel through them in safety, by night and by day’” (p. 246).

We stressed earlier that an authentic tradition continually gives rise to rebirth, and that the reverse is equally true. A tradition cannot really be handed down unless each person who receives it undergoes a new birth—a spiritual birth (wilâdat rûhânîya). Such a birth consists precisely in discovering and making one's own the spiritual meaning which, as we have just seen, our authors distinguish so firmly from the outward and passing circumstances that concern historical faith (fides historica).

Every new spiritual birth thus brings forth a new understanding of the tradition: it renews the tradition itself. This is what the opponents of the Shaykhi school failed to grasp. The journey “in safety, by night and by day” is what we might call the tradition's hermeneutic expansion: the continuing unfolding of its meaning. Innovation breaks with tradition. Renewal, on the other hand, is inseparable from it. There can be no tradition without perpetual renewal; the very idea of tradition carries with it the idea of rebirth.

We have just quoted a few lines from a work that Shaykh Ahmad gave the simple title Teachings (Fawâ'id). Some critics have suggested that he understood neither the aims nor the vocabulary of the philosophers. We have argued, on the contrary, that he knew perfectly well what was distinctive about his own teaching and terminology. It is therefore necessary to offer a brief account of his metaphysical doctrine. This cannot pretend to be a synthesis.
But a very concise summary of the first chapters of the Teachings will be enough to show that Shaykhi thought amounts to a genuine reform and renewal of metaphysics.

The Teachings has a history of its own. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î first wrote a twelve-chapter treatise under this unassuming title, around 1225/1810, as he returned from Isfahan to Yazd. Its extreme brevity makes it almost impenetrable to a reader who lacks the key. Some eight years later, a shaykh who was his friend asked him for that key as they traveled together on pilgrimage to Mecca. A journey may not have been the ideal moment to ask someone to write another book.

Yet the long stages of the pilgrimage evidently afforded ample opportunity for dictation, and Shaykh Ahmad rose admirably to the occasion. The result was a remarkable clarification, completed on 9 Shawwâl 1233 / 13 October 1818. The original text and its commentary together make up a large octavo volume of 290 pages. The shaykh divides his original work into short passages, or lemmata, of a few lines each, and follows each with a commentary resolving the difficulties presented by “those things which will seem strange in comparison with what theologians and philosophers ('olamâ and hokamâ) are accustomed to discussing nowadays, and which I am the first to take up, though our Imams and the foremost of their Shiites have always discussed them.” A Persian disciple of the shaykh, Mohammad ibn Mohammad Nâsir Gîlânî, had attended his lessons for several years.

We have so far been unable to discover anything about him beyond what he tells us himself. The twelve Fawâ'id formed part of the teaching he received, and he wrote his own commentary on them, insisting that he did no more than transcribe his master's oral instruction. We were fortunate enough to find the sole surviving copy of this commentary—which is also the author's own manuscript—in a private collection in Tehran, belonging to Mr. Soltânî. Neither teacher nor disciple seems to have known of the commentary that the other was writing. Comparing the two is therefore all the more revealing, and opens up far-reaching lines of inquiry. Shaykh Ahmad's own written commentary is clearer and more precise; the disciple's, however, preserves digressions to which the shaykh did not return in his own version.

With these two commentaries, the twelve chapters ultimately form a veritable summa of Imami metaphysics. We hope to publish a translation of Shaykh Ahmad's text and his own commentary elsewhere. For now, we shall confine ourselves to a short account of the first five chapters.

The first chapter sets out three kinds of argument or proof, each with its own intellectual, spiritual, and moral requirements: dialectical proof (dalîl al-mojâdala), supported by theoretical knowledge; exhortative proof (dalîl al-maw'iza), supported by the heart (qalb); and the proof of wisdom (dalîl al-hikma), supported by the innermost heart, its center (fu'âd). “The first condition of the proof of wisdom is that you act faithfully toward your Lord. For when you reflect and contemplate by means of that proof, you summon your Lord to appear before you, while at the same time He summons you to appear before the very center of your heart. As the First Imam said: ‘Our representations cannot encompass Him, yet He manifests Himself to them through themselves.

“But through those same representations He also withholds Himself from them, and summons them to appear before themselves.’ Your Lord then enters into contention with you. Weigh, therefore, with the just Balance. This is the best ta'wîl, the best spiritual interpretation (cf. Qur'an 17:37).

“The second condition is that you stop where evidence is evident to you, where understanding is intelligible to you, where the explanation is one you can communicate. This accords with the divine command: ‘Do not seek knowledge of what it is not possible for you to know: your hearing, your sight, the center of your heart—these are what will be called to account’ (17:38).

“The third condition is that you regard all these situations with God's eye, not your own [...]—that is, with the eye that is His own description of Himself to you and for you: as He makes Himself known to you, as He characterizes Himself for you. This means that your existing, considered as your act of being—your existence—is a trace and a light: the state of the knowledge you have of yourself ...” (§§23–27). Already in this first chapter the shaykh develops his fundamental positions: his doctrine of the forms of manifestation and the degrees of consciousness and knowledge. His vocabulary of being also begins to take shape, marking a break with the customary language of the philosophers.

Chapter II takes the demands and implications of Shiite negative theology—the refusal to attribute creaturely qualities to God—to their furthest limit. The source of being transcends every category of being. No attribute can be assigned to it, since every attribute belongs to the order of creatures; every description already presupposes being, and therefore always arrives too late. God is at once the Known and the Unknown, the Present and the Absent. The only way He can be known is through the very fact that He cannot be known. For any positive knowledge of Him comes through an act of knowing in which He is never the object, but always the active subject. He can be known only as He makes Himself known, each time, to the person who recognizes Him.

“Nothing comes forth from pre-eternity, nothing enters it, nothing reaches it that would make it possible to announce or describe what is there. Since this is so, no one knows anything of Him except that by which He describes Himself—which means that anyone other than He does not know Him. He alone knows the depths of His own essence, because His knowledge of Himself is His very essence. When, therefore, He describes Himself, the description given by the Divine Being to the Divine Being is divine; but the description He gives of Himself reaches us in the condition of created things. We ourselves are therefore that description, which reaches us through ourselves. It is through us that God makes Himself known to us.

“Thus His description of Himself for a creature is itself a created thing. For what is created knows only what is created ... A being knows only what belongs to the same order as itself” (§§84–91). “To say that the dimension in which He can be known is His very unknowability means that a being is known and understood only through something of its own kind ... Thus the Necessary Being is known by the fact that He has no quality, no likeness, no equal; that the depths of His essence are unknowable; that one knows only His self-description; that no knowledge can encompass Him. Everything that can be known is other than He.

“All one knows, then, is that no path leads to the depths of His Essence, or to knowledge of His self-description. Our only knowledge of Him is our not knowing. This is how He makes Himself known to us, for we know only what resembles ourselves. He is the Necessarily Necessary, while remaining the absolutely Unknowable. This is what is designated as the pure Essence [...], for every consideration made from a particular point of view is an interpretation belonging to the created order. Such interpretations really concern His abodes or stations of manifestation, which are never empty or inactive anywhere” (§§99, 101–105, 114).

This metaphysics of being has affinities with that of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî and Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, as well as with Ismaili metaphysics. It maintains a radical difference in meaning between divine and created being. The Necessary Being, who possesses being in its fullness, eludes all description, since any description presupposes being and therefore applies only to a being that has been given leave to be, a being set free to exist.

Hence the break with the philosophers' usual vocabulary. Philosophers have generally treated “necessary being,” “being as such,” and “absolute being” as equivalent expressions. The shaykh rejects that equivalence because, in his view, it misses the very question that first philosophy should be asking.

Continuing in the same direction, the shaykh reveals himself in Chapter III as a metaphysician of rare depth. When philosophers speak of “absolute being” and identify it with God, they generally believe they have reached a concept at the utmost limit, beyond which thought cannot ascend.

But the qualification absolute (motlaq) has the form of a passive participle. It therefore implies, by its very nature, an active agent that absolves or releases being: an act that sets being free to cross (jawâz) all the barriers of nonbeing. Here Latin is particularly helpful in expressing Shaykh Ahmad's thought.

In the concept of absolute being (wojûd motlaq), that being is absolved because it presupposes an absolvens, one who releases it from nonbeing in the first place. This absolvens (motliq) puts being into the imperative mood—KN = Esto, “Be!”, not fiat, “Let it be!”—although the sufficient reason for this commanding preference for being over nothingness will never be accessible to our reason. If what truly is is the absolvens, then even at the highest level we can reach, we encounter only being that has been released by it. And this absolutum, this absolute being, belongs from the outset to the created order. What truly is therefore remains beyond our category of being: superbeing, hyperousia.

“Absolute being,” then, means something different here from what philosophers ordinarily mean by it. The shaykh lists some eighteen equivalent symbolic names for it: the eternal Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya), the First Delimitation, Universal Mercy, the Universal Tree, the Primal Will, the letter Kâf closing the circle upon itself, absolute walâyat (the spiritual authority and guardianship of the Imams), the Word before which the Great Abyss withdraws, Essential Love, and others.

This leads him into a searching analysis of mashî'at, the divine Primal Will. He shows that in the creative Act, mashî'at is at once the subject, the object, and the purpose of that act, as well as its matter, form, and instrument. The Primal Will thus appears as a primordial, metaphysical Adam (Adam al-akbar, the Greater Adam, or Homo maximus). It is the zenith of which Adam “our father,” who came into being without father or mother, is the nadir in the world of our earthly history.

The eternal Primal Will is the primordial Adam, “the first of the Adams” (awwal al-âdamîyîn); and Eve, this Adam's equal, is the release of being (jawâz, itlâq), absolute being—that is, being absolved from nonbeing, from the Great Abyss. In this primordial heavenly Adam, Matter and Form each exist in their own right and, at the same time, through one another. In Adam “our father,” by contrast, they exist through the divine Act and then successively through each other. After Adam, being propagates through the “nuptial union” of matter and form.

“The nadir of the divine Primal Will is our father Adam, for he had no father or mother other than himself. He came into existence from himself alone, and from him the human race came into being through nuptial union and successive generations. Likewise the Primal Will has no father or mother other than itself, and from it things come into being through nuptial union and successive generations. When we say of Adam that he had ‘no father or mother other than himself,’ we mean that Adam was born of his own Matter, which is the father, and of his own Form, which is the mother [...]. The Primal Will is the primordial Adam; the Eve of this Adam is the freedom to be (the absolution of being).

“Eve is therefore Adam's equal, neither more nor less than he” (§§159–160, 164). And in his commentary the shaykh explains: “Adam is the nadir of this Primal Will because the Will itself is the First Adam. It is composed of matter and form. Its matter is light, while its form is the temple of tawhîd, divine oneness. Adam's father was his matter, and his mother was his form [...]. When I say that Eve is the equal of this Adam, I mean that there is nothing possible to which the Primal Will is not joined, and conversely nothing in the Primal Will that remains outside the possible.”

Here we can already see a fundamental transformation of Aristotelian hylomorphism, the doctrine of matter and form. The terms “matter” (hylê, mâdda) and “form” (morphê, sûrat) remain, but their roles have been reversed.

In contrast to the association suggested by our Indo-European words materia and mater (“mother”), matter here is the father and form is the mother. This is one of Shaykh Ahmad's central theses, always present in his thought. He is well aware that he is reversing both the vocabulary and the conceptual order of the philosophers. Matter here is light: being itself, the act of existing. Form is quiddity—what a thing is—the dimension of shadow that fixes, determines, and delimits that light. It is form that gives birth to the new being. The shaykh will often speak of being as metaphysical “matter.” Few things have more surprised his critics.
But rather than declare that he failed to understand the philosophers, we would do better to try to understand precisely what he is saying, and the language in which he says it.

Chapter IV examines the creative Act, the divine act of bringing things into being (fi'l), as we have already defined it: the act accessible to us in the way “God reveals Himself to us through ourselves.”

Considered as the self-manifestation of divine Energy, the creative Act can be analyzed into four moments or phases. Together they form a unity called Mercy, Rahma, whose role is reminiscent of Sophia in other theosophical traditions and which here is the metaphysical androgyne, Adam-and-Eve. This “universal divine Mercy” is indeed one of the names, one of the ways of conceiving absolute being: being that the creative Act has released and set free to exist.

When the shaykh writes, in language faintly recalling alchemy, that “God took four parts of the moisture of Mercy by means of that very moisture,” the four parts are simply Mercy itself. Mercy is what takes hold, what is taken hold of, the means by which it is taken hold of, and that from which it is taken. Grammatically speaking, it is as though the roles assigned separately to the nominative, accusative, instrumental, and ablative cases all belonged to one and the same reality. This places us as far from creation ex nihilo as from a theory of emanation.

As for the fourfold structure into which the act of divine creation can be analyzed, its first two phases are mashî'at, the divine Primal Will concerned with calling being into existence (kawn), and irâda, the act of willing concerned with determining being ('ayn)—with what a being is in the very act of existing. These first two phases make up what the shaykh calls “first creation” (khalq awwal), or “first quiddity” (mâhîya).

The third and fourth phases are qadar or taqdîr, the act that apportions to each individual being its proper measure, its own share (the handasa îjâdîya, an “existence-giving geometry” that structures being in each individual instance), and qazâ, the “decree” that brings this apportionment into full effect. Together these last two phases constitute “second creation” (khalq thânî), or second quiddity. Between the first and second creations, however, an event takes place that gives this metaphysics of being the character of a metaphysical drama. A question is put to the primordial Adam and repeated at every level of the universe: A-lasto bi-rabbi-kom?—“Am I not your Lord?” (Qur'an 7:171).

In a sense, this pre-existent questioning plays the same role as the prelude to Plato's Gorgias. According to the answer they give—ranging from genuine assent to a refusal disguised as “yes”—the human beings pre-existing within this cosmic Adam choose their own destiny: their quiddity, the measure and capacities of their being. They choose, in other words, whether they will experience their existence in this world as an act of Mercy or an act of Wrath. The seeming contradiction between “predestination” and responsibility is overcome, because a person's responsibility is engaged by an act that the person performed before earthly existence.

We find the same fourfold pattern at every stage and level of Shaykh Ahmad's analysis of the cosmos and of the human being. It appears, for instance, in his explanation of the symbolism of the Throne ('Arsh), with its four pillars, four colors, and four archangels. It also embraces the pattern employed in the philosophical science of the alphabet, or science of letters ('ilm al-horûf). Shaykh Ahmad therefore makes a long digression into this difficult discipline, in which our theosophers share the interests of the Kabbalists. The digression culminates in a return to the doctrine that identifies being (wojûd) with Light (nûr) and quiddity with the shadow that receives the light and brings forth its manifestation. As we have said, this is the doctrine that determines his understanding of “matter” and “form,” overturning the traditional vocabulary of hylomorphism while still retaining its terms.
This is the central theme of Chapter V. Its first part is devoted to the various “series” or “sets” of universes presented in Sadûq's Khisâl.

What does it mean to speak of two, three, four, five, or six worlds—the six days of Creation—then seven, eight, and so on, up to twelve universes? Here we encounter again certain themes already discussed in connection with Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. We also see Shaykh Ahmad's concepts become more precise: “spiritual matter” (mâdda ma'nawîya) as “molten Light” (Nûr dhâ'ib), and “elemental matter” (mâdda 'onsorîya) as “frozen” or “solidified Light” (jâmid). This enables him to take a highly original position in relation to Majlisî on tajarrod, separation or immateriality (Greek khôrismos). For the great official theologian of Shiism, complete separation or immateriality can apply only to God.

There can be no “separate” substance other than God, and Majlisî comes close to declaring unbelievers—pronouncing takfîr upon—philosophers who apply tajarrod to other beings. Shaykh Ahmad maintains, however, that only certain Islamic philosophers are open to this charge, and that Majlisî's condemnation does not touch the theosophers who remain faithful to the Imams' teaching. This position is characteristic of a particular current within Shiism. The First Intelligence has its own “matter,” just as a mineral has matter.

But the Light that constitutes being undergoes countless degrees of “condensation,” so the Intelligence differs from a mineral as heaven differs from earth, without there being any need to speak of tajarrod in the strict sense. Our theosophers thus meet certain later Western Neoplatonists whose thought has been described as “Christian materialism.” It would be more accurate to call it “spiritual realism,” a view for which the opposition between materialism and spiritualism no longer has meaning. (We have in mind, once again, Robert Fludd and the Cambridge Platonists.) Already we can discern, in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î as in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, certain enduring lines of thought within traditional Persian philosophy, from the Safavid to the Qajar period.

As the preceding chapter has shown, Shaykh Ahmad often expresses his metaphysics of being through an account of Adam—an Adamology. In this fifth Fâ'ida we learn to distinguish three “Adams” in the spiritual world, which is “pre-Adamic” in relation to “Adam our father.” The first is the Greater Adam (Adam al-akbar, Homo maximus): the divine Primal Will (mashî'at) and the “Heaven of absolute walâyat.” The second Adam is the “Muhammadan Light” (Nûr Mohammadî), with its fourteen beings of light.

The third is the Universal Intelligence, the Intelligence of that Light, whose “children” are the individual intelligences. Their relationships are complex. From this Adamology follows the teaching on matter and form which, as we have seen, overturns classical hylomorphism. Matter becomes the masculine element, the “father,” while Form or quiddity becomes the feminine element, the “mother,” receiving the amount of matter appropriate to its own specification. The consequences are revolutionary, extending from mineralogy to aesthetics, and even more immediately to anthropology and the doctrine of the Imams.

In contrast to the Aristotelian-Thomist tradition, it is Form here, not matter, that provides the principle of individuation. “At the level of sensory perception, matter is individualized by the imaginal Form (sûrat mithâlîya). As for Form, although it belongs to the imaginal world, it appears to sensory perception through its conjunction with elemental matters. But this conjunction holds in the invisible, suprasensible world (ghayb) of the Intelligences as much as in the visible world of material bodies. It applies to the outer world and also to thoughts themselves.

“Thus, in the true sense worth seeking to know, being or existence, wherever something other than God is concerned, is matter (mâdda). This is the correct position, contrary to what the majority of philosophers maintain” (§265). In other words, the claim is not that some previously existing matter is being. It is that being, the act of existing, is matter—and that this matter which is being is itself light. “For if being were something other than matter, its definition would be incomplete without that other thing.
“But being is the most evident of all things: it is its own definition. Being is the matter of things, because it is what is most evident in every thing.

“Yet precisely because its self-evidence is so overwhelming, being remains hidden from most people. They imagine it to be an object of pure thought, a mere concept; or they take it as the copula in a logical judgment; or they identify it with what truly is. All these opinions are mistaken. The truth is that being which has a beginning is, in each thing, the matter proportionate to that thing.

“But what truly is, no one knows except itself. Every doctrine is therefore false that makes it the root of being, or makes being its shadow. There can be no conceptual participation here (analogia entis), because the sacred, transcendent divine Selfhood (Dhât moqadassa) cannot fall under an essence held in common with anything else. There can be no analogia entis, no common proportion between the divine Selfhood and anything whatsoever” (ibid.). This is exactly the doctrine of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, as we have already noted.

“As for the technical vocabulary used by the ancients and the philosophers, when they held that Form is the father while matter is the mother, they did so because they believed that a being's growth and acquisition of character (takhalloq) take place within matter, making matter the mother. Nothing could be further from the true relation of things. That matter is the father and Form the mother, on the other hand, follows from the sayings of the Imams. Take, for example, this saying of Imam Ja'far: ‘God created the faithful believers from His Light and dyed them in His Mercy. This is why one believer is the brother of another through his father and mother. His father is Light and his mother is Mercy’” (§267).

When we say that a ring is made of silver, we mean that the silver entering into it is the matter from which it is made. To say that a believer was created from Light is to say that Light is the matter; and it is this Light that the Imam calls the believer's father. “If we adopt the philosophers' definition of the human being as a ‘thinking living being’ (hayawân nâtiq), then the light is the share of living nature (hissa hayawânîya), and mercy the share of thinking nature (hissa nâtiqîya). Living-being is matter; thinking-being is Form. By matter we mean being, existing: the first thing emanating from the divine creative Act, since only one thing emanates from that Act. Form is the configuration that shapes this Emanation into the multiplicity of its specifications and individual beings” (§273).

We have deliberately included these lengthy quotations in order to place Shaykh Ahmad's fundamental criticism of the usual definition of the human being as hayawân nâtiq—the thinking or “speaking” animal, animal rationale—in its proper setting. The supposed unity of an animal genus, evolving through successive forms from protozoan to human being, is merely a logical concept, a construct of the mind. Matter does not receive Form. Rather, Form receives, in each case, the amount of matter suited to it, and Form gives birth to the new being. It is impossible to classify or define the human being as a variation within the animal genus, because of the drama that intervenes between first creation or quiddity and second creation or quiddity (see above).

There is a vital reality (hayawânîya) elaborated in the celestial Spheres (falakîya). This reality belongs to animals as an essential constituent, but for the human being it is only accidental. The human essence is instead the spiritual vital reality of the malakût, the spiritual world (h. qodsîya malakûtîya). More than this, the Imam—that is, each of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”—possesses a divine spiritual vital reality (h. q. ilâhîya). The human reality, the spiritual life proper to humanity, stands in relation to this divine reality as animal existence stands in relation to human existence. Just as the “animal” condition is accidental to what makes a human being human, so the human condition is accidental to the Imam's divine spiritual reality.

Hence the idea of a hypostatic union between the Imam's divine spiritual nature (malakûtî lahûtî) and human nature, insofar as the latter shares the biological reality of this world, is inconceivable. What can be considered, in any case, is the human reality as a living being of the malakût, at the level of a caro spiritualis, a spiritual body. Then what takes place is an epiphany of the Imam's lâhût, his divine dimension, within the human malakût. This is the scene described at the beginning of the tradition of the White Cloud. We might say that whereas Christology revolves around the union of two natures, divine and human, the decisions reached by Imamology depend on the idea of a threefold nature, as outlined above.

Comparative theology and theosophy have here a vast, still unexplored field of inquiry, and this alone would justify speaking of a “renewal.” But in using that word in the heading to these pages, we were thinking first of the renewal of the very problems of metaphysics when the doctrine of the Imams becomes its guiding principle. We have seen enough of this without taking the analysis of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's Fawâ'id any further. The doctrine of the Imams provides the horizon for the mind's highest speculations.

For that very reason it also determines the distinctive character of the Shaykhi community within Shiism. The teaching of the Imams points to the existence of a hidden spiritual hierarchy, whose highest members can be present in this world only incognito for as long as the Imam remains in occultation (ghaybat). This concerns what the Shaykhi school calls the “fourth pillar” (rokn râbi') of its doctrine. Behind it we can discern, almost as through a transparent veil, the idea of a certain ideal brotherhood familiar from the esoteric traditions of the West.
We must spend a few pages on this teaching, since it was unfortunately among those that provoked the most criticism, precisely because it was misunderstood or not understood at all.

At the end of the preceding section we again used the word ghaybat, which properly denotes the occultation, or hiddenness, of the Twelfth Imam—the Imam of our time, the Hidden Imam. Among Shiite spiritual masters, however, the meaning of the word sometimes widens to include the suprasensible, secret dimension of beings and things: their spiritual form. This dimensio mystica, or mystical dimension, then becomes the key to hierognosis, a form of spiritual awareness that perceives realities in their proper forms. Nothing belonging to the worlds beyond ours is frozen or reduced to our habitual ways of imagining things, or brought under the control of religions concerned with worldly power.

Shaykhi theosophy rests on four pillars (rokn): divine unity, the doctrine of prophecy, the doctrine of the Imams, and the Shiite community. There is nothing novel here in comparison with the program of Shiite religious books generally; it accords entirely with the Imams' teaching. At the same time, this fourfold plan indicates how a complete account of Shaykhi Shiite theosophy would have to be organized. The doctrine of the Imams would be the keystone of the whole structure.

For the fullness of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” is understood and contemplated first of all in a sphere of existence ontologically prior to the brief appearance of their individual earthly persons. This fullness constitutes the world of lâhût, the divine dimension, at the very first flowering of being. As pre-cosmic entities, the “persons of light” of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are the acts of primordial divine self-manifestation, or theophany. They are the divine Names and Attributes, the only aspect of divinity that can be known to us; they are the divine instruments of creation, its “operations at work,” the agents of cosmogony.

Ontologically “below” the world of lâhût lie the worlds traditionally called Jabarût, Malakût, and Molk, the last being our world as it appears to the senses. All these universes correspond symbolically to one another. An adequate understanding of the human being must therefore encompass them all. It includes the structure of the human being's fourfold body; the idea of an archetypal subtle body, the jism hurqalyî (the body on the plane of Hûrqalyâ, closely related to Proclus's okhêma, the subtle vehicle of the soul); and, intimately connected with this subtle physiology, the conception of Heaven and Hell as realities within the human being. These are central themes of the doctrine, both in its “physics” of the Resurrection and in its understanding of visionary experiences such as the Prophet's mi'râj, his heavenly ascent.

Since we have discussed these subjects at some length elsewhere, we shall do no more than mention them here. Needless to say, Shaykhi thought draws upon a remarkably powerful metaphysical imagination, unquestionably nourished by the transmitted sayings (akhbâr) of the holy Imams. This imaginative reach exceeds the capacities of those interlocutors whose learning is confined to fiqh, the purely legal science. Such a disparity of intellectual and spiritual levels usually has disastrous consequences for constructive discussion.

The “fourth pillar,” which has provoked so much writing and controversy in Iran, provides an example. Yet this article of Shaykhi doctrine does nothing more than give effect to a precept of the Imams expressed through two traditional terms: tawallâ, sympathetic attachment and allegiance to someone; and tabarrâ, aversion, repudiation, and separation. As noted above, the texts decisively settle whether Mohammad Karîm-Khân “invented” this doctrine. He did not. The principle of the fourth pillar was taught by his predecessors, and on this point Shaykhi teaching shows complete continuity.

We can trace the idea at least as far back as Nasîroddîn Tûsî, and further still. It means that the bond of spiritual allegiance uniting every Shiite, every follower, to the Imam also demands solidarity and loyalty toward all those joined by that same allegiance to the Imam, in a hierarchy of spiritual degrees.

Here a characteristically Twelver Shiite idea comes into view, one that can exist only within Twelver Shiism because it is determined specifically by the ghaybat, the Imam's occultation. The fourth pillar concerns the shape and structure of the Shiite community. Rooted in the esoteric idea underlying the shî'a and tashayyo'—Shiite allegiance and identity—it shows that its adherents fully understand what the Imam's occultation entails. It rules out turning the spiritual into a social institution, or giving spiritual forms and hierarchies an outward, material embodiment that would identify them with the established organizations of visible history.

The only structure compatible with it is a spiritual fellowship, an Ecclesia spiritualis, a spiritual community. The hierarchy of its members can never be known or recognized from outside. The spiritual qualification that determines its degrees has nothing to do with secular claims or temporal functions; it lies beyond the reach of sociology. It remains a personal, secret gift bestowed by the Imam.

This means acknowledging both spiritual beings superior to this world and, among human beings, a hierarchy based solely on spiritual worth—on greater or lesser spiritual closeness to the Imam. Its members can never invoke that rank publicly, since it is not directed toward exercising power in or over this world. The hierarchy itself remains hidden within the esoteric community and cannot be equated with the positions of outward authority that necessarily arise in the organization of a community here below. A thorough study would need to draw on several major Shaykhi works. Here we shall simply set out the state of the question, following the indications in Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's book, to which we now return (pp. 95–143).

All Shiites agree that three kinds of knowledge are indispensable pillars of religion in its fullness: knowledge of divine unity (tawhîd); knowledge of the prophetic mission in general (nobowwat), and especially of the last Prophet; and knowledge of Hazrat Fâtima and the Twelve Imams.

But the building could not stand without a fourth pillar: to be in friendship and communion with all the friends of these august Persons, to separate oneself from all who separate themselves from them, and to have nothing in common with their enemies. This is the injunction expressed by tawallâ and tabarrâ, explained above. The only difference of opinion is that some Shiite scholars regard this solidarity as one of the practical consequences (forû') of religious faith, while others count it among its principles and foundations (osûl). The Shaykhis take the latter view, and the lineage of this teaching can be traced at least to Shaykh Mofîd (d. 413/1022) (p. 104). Conscious solidarity and fellowship with all the friends of the Imams, the Awliyâ, together with separation from their enemies: that is the fourth pillar, the IVe rokn. Who, then, are these Awliyâ?

Everyone recognizes that some people are more spiritually perfected than others, closer to God than others. Within this elite there must also be degrees of knowledge, spiritual awareness, and devotion. The Qur'an calls them the ashâb al-yamîn, “companions of the right”; the sâbiqûn, “those who go before”; the moqarrabûn, “those brought near”; and so forth. Already in the Imams' own time there were remarkable individuals endowed with profound knowledge and perfected spirituality; such people have continued to appear ever since. Outstanding examples include Salmân Pârsî, Abu Dharr, the two Jâbirs, Mofazzal, and the last two nâ'ib—deputies—of the Twelfth Imam during the “minor occultation” (ghaybat-e soghrâ): Hosayn ibn Rûh Nawbakhtî and 'Alî ibn Mohammad Samarrî. At the latter's death in 329/940, the “major occultation” (ghaybat-e kobrâ) began.

The Imam's gaze rested upon all these men, and each received certain mystical and visionary gifts from him. Shiites recognize them all as guides acting on the Imam's behalf, and accept that others like them may still enter the Imam's presence, even during the major occultation—in other words, in our own day. The fourth pillar's bond of friendship and solidarity embraces the whole succession of these Awliyâ, invisibly succeeding one another from century to century. That they are guides and intermediaries is the meaning given to Qur'an 34:17 by Shiite interpretation. Knowledge of this category of higher beings is as necessary as knowledge of each of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” (pp. 107–110).

But we now live in the time of the great ghaybat, the major occultation. After seventy years of minor occultation, the last nâ'ib—the Imam's deputy or representative—received an order from the Imam himself not to invest anyone else with that office (see Book VII below). “The matter now belongs to God”: these were the last words of 'Alî al-Samarrî, the Imam's final deputy, as he was dying.

In inaugurating the major occultation, the Great Absence, those words gave the Shiite spiritual outlook its particular tone, that desperatio fiducialis which is despair sustained by trust, a pessimism alive with hope. At the same time they transferred the whole structure of the Shiite community to the invisible spiritual plane. From that point on, the figure of the Hidden Imam dominates the horizon of Shiite consciousness—or rather, he is the very history of that consciousness. The meaning of this history is therefore utterly different from what our modern dogmatists call the “meaning of history.”

Just as the Imam exists but remains hidden in a world beyond our dialectical constructions and ready-made certainties, so the spiritual hierarchies emanating from his Person, and in a sense shaped by him, have never ceased to exist. They remain hidden with him until his final Epiphany. It is not, therefore, that the Bâb (“threshold” of the Imam) and the nâ'ib have ceased to exist. They exist, but are hidden, rigorously concealed in an inviolable anonymity, just as the Imam exists yet remains the “Hidden Imam” until his final manifestation, or parousia. The underlying principle had already been developed by Suhrawardi in the prologue to his Oriental Theosophy: earthly humanity, indeed our world itself, could not persist in existence for a single instant if the mystical pole (the Hidden Imam) were no longer there, together with all his invisible Companions, the Friends who from generation to generation are the “Perfect Shiites.”
